props.title: Looney Tunes: Back in Action
props.initialSlug: Bugs Bunny joins human spy duo in zany adventure

sections.content: Looney Tunes: Back in Action (2003) represents Joe Dante's ambitious attempt to merge live-action with Warner Bros.' classic animated characters, following the template of Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988). Dante, known for Gremlins (1984) and Small Soldiers (1998), brings his signature blend of anarchic humor and pop culture commentary. The film pairs Brendan Fraser with Daffy Duck in a globe-trotting adventure that deliberately channels the manic energy of Chuck Jones's original cartoons while satirizing Hollywood's corporate culture and spy movie conventions.

sections.content: The film's most impressive sequences showcase director Dante's encyclopedic knowledge of classic animation. The Louvre chase scene specifically references countless Warner Bros. cartoons while incorporating surreal art history jokes, with characters jumping in and out of famous paintings. This technique echoes similar moments in The Purple Rose of Cairo (1985) and Last Action Hero (1993), where the boundary between reality and fiction becomes delightfully fluid.

Despite its box office disappointment, Looney Tunes: Back in Action stands as one of the most faithful adaptations of the classic Warner Bros. cartoon style. Unlike Space Jam (1996), which relied heavily on its basketball premise, Back in Action embraces the fourth-wall-breaking chaos and rapid-fire gags that defined the original shorts. The film's meta-commentary on Warner Bros.' corporate structure - with Steve Martin playing the literally cartoon-evil studio chairman - shows remarkable prescience about Hollywood's increasingly corporate nature. sections.content: The film's technical achievements in blending animation with live action built upon techniques pioneered by Mary Poppins (1964) and perfected in Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988). Dante's team pushed these boundaries further, creating seamless interactions between Fraser and the animated characters while maintaining the distinctive "squash and stretch" physics of classic Warner Bros. animation. This attention to cartoon authenticity distinguishes it from contemporaries like The Adventures of Rocky and Bullwinkle (2000).
